messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Navy Officer
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 33

**Vignette: Lieutenant James Miller**

Lieutenant James Miller reports to his therapy sessions in full uniform, though he has taken to leaving the top button undone—a detail his wife, Sarah, pointed out as uncharacteristic. At 34, James has served as a surface warfare officer for twelve years, known among his crew for steady hands and a calm voice over the bridge. That calm was tested three years ago, when his ship, the USS *Ardent*, sailed directly into Super Typhoon Kalmaegi during a routine patrol in the Philippine Sea.

James remembers the sequence in fragments that return without warning. The sea state had escalated from heavy to catastrophic in under four hours. He was the tactical action officer on watch when the first rogue wave struck the port beam, rolling the ship to nearly forty degrees. He remembers gripping the console, shouting orders to adjust course, and then the sound of metal groaning from the forward berthing—a sound he later learned was a stack of lockers tearing loose, pinning a petty officer against a bulkhead. James directed damage control teams while the ship pitched through wave after wave. Two sailors were injured; one required emergency surgery in the wardroom. For eighteen hours, James did not leave the bridge. When the storm finally passed, he completed the after-action report, visited the injured in medical, and called Sarah to say he was safe. He told himself he was fine.

He is not fine.

In the months following the typhoon, James found himself replaying specific moments: the sensation of the deck falling away beneath his feet, the high-pitched whine of the ship’s hull under stress, the sight of the petty officer’s blood mixing with seawater on the deck. At first, these images only came at night. He would wake in their Virginia Beach apartment drenched in sweat, his heart hammering, unable to speak. Sarah would hold him until he stopped shaking. But then the intrusions began to surface during the day. A sudden gust of wind rattling the window would send him into a freeze. The sound of a pressure washer at the carwash—a sound that resembles water hitting steel—makes him flinch so hard he has nearly dropped his grocery bags. He avoids the pier on windy days now, even though his current billet is ashore as a training officer. He tells himself it’s just fatigue.

At work, James is functional but brittle. He completes his training plans with meticulous care, but he has stopped volunteering for sea duty. He cannot bring himself to board a small boat for a routine port visit. His commanding officer noticed a change in his risk tolerance—James now adds extra safety briefings, double-checks every navigational chart, and becomes visibly irritated when junior officers treat weather forecasts casually. He snaps at a lieutenant who jokes about “riding out a storm.” Later, in his office, he stares at his hands and feels ashamed. He has started drinking two beers every night, then three on weekends, to quiet the hypervigilance.

At home, James is distant. He and Sarah wanted children; now he cannot imagine bringing a child into a world he cannot predict. He feels estranged from her, even as she tries to draw him out. When she asks about his day, he gives one-word answers. Intimacy has dwindled—he feels a restless, churning anxiety in his chest that makes softness impossible. He spent last month’s leave watching weather radar loops on his phone, waiting for another storm that never came.

James scored a 33 on the PCL-5, endorsing moderate symptoms. He sought help only after Sarah told him she was “running out of ideas” and that she missed the man she married. He came to the first session with a notebook, ready to take notes, as if therapy were another briefing. But when the therapist asks him to describe the typhoon, he cannot finish. His eyes go distant. He says, “I should have done more,” and then he is quiet for a long time, listening to the rain against the window.
